name: Bini
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Wescott, Roger W. 1962. A Bini Grammar, Part 1: Phonology. East Lansing: African Language and Area Center, Michigan State University. (ERIC ED003870; archive.org eric-microfiche scan.)
catalog_locator: Chapter 2, Section 3 'Stress', print pp. 30-33; Section 7 'Prosodic Phonemes', print pp. 56-57.
catalog_quote: Section 3: Stress. Let us begin by defining stress as variable loudness of vowel-articulation. Although it has no phonemic stress, Bini, like all other known languages, does have phonetic stress; and, once assessed, this stress can serve as a valuable phonic clue to syllabification and intonation. Bini stress correlates positively with the following five phonic factors, listed in order of importance: 5 glide (tone-shift) 4 pitch (tone-height) 3 quantity (vowel-length) 2 sonority (openness ov vowel) 1 priority of occurrence. Each of these five factors, in turn, contains sub-orders within itself. Thus, if we give a single level-toned vowel the stress value of 1, vowels carrying tone-glides (shifts from one tone-level to another) can be variously rated with stress values from 2 to 6 ... [p. 32] Fifth, stress varies directly as order of occurrence in an utterance. Thus, in a word like ágágá, "many chairs", where other relevant conditions [p. 33] (i.e., level, pitch, length, and sonority) are equal, the first a gets the most stress, the intermediate a intermediate stress, and the last a least stress. Vowel quality (i.e., orality or nasality) seems to have no correlation, either positive or negative, with stress. ... [p. 56] Bini, like Ibo (but unlike Yoruba), is what Welmers calls a terrace-tone language.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Edo/Bini is a tone language (Wescott: six phonemic tones; later authors: two tones plus downstep) with no phonemic (contrastive or positionally fixed) word stress; perceived loudness is a phonetic by-product of tone glides, pitch height, vowel length and vowel openness, with a weak default for earlier syllables in an utterance to be louder when all else is equal.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; stress is treated as gradient phonetic loudness (a 1-6 scale), not as primary/secondary word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Low tone carries the most loudness because of its subphonemic down-glide (p. 56); vowel nasality has no effect on loudness; English loans develop vowel colour next to the syllable that bore English primary stress (p. 105-106). Note the contradictory older claim in Thomas 1910: 141 ('The dynamic accent falls normally on the penultimate, but in words ending in ia, ie, oa, ua, etc., it usually falls on the antepenultimate'), a pre-tonal-analysis impression not upheld by any later linguist (Melzian 1937 leaves stress unmarked; Emovon 1979, Adeniyi 2007, Ogie 2009, Omozuwa 1989/1991 describe Edo purely as a two-tone language and say nothing about word stress).
new_statements.domain_note: Wescott's 'priority of occurrence' factor is stated over the utterance/breath-group (loudness declines with declination), not as a word-level rule; his examples are citation words and short phrases.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Edo proper (Bini) of Benin City, glottocode bini1246 / ISO bin; Wescott and Melzian use the name 'Bini', Thomas 'Edo (Bini)'. Thomas 1910 Part II also covers other Edoid varieties (Ishan, Kukuruku etc.) but the quoted accent passage is in the 'Edo grammar' section and refers to Edo (Bini) unless otherwise stated (his footnote p. 132).

new_statements.relation_note: This is the very source behind the existing statement (Wescott 1962 p. 30), so the placement reading is the same: no phonemic word stress, language tonal. The re-read supplies the truncated continuation (the five phonic correlates of phonetic loudness, the earlier-is-louder rule) and the Section 7 note that low tone is phonetically the loudest tone. The catalog record for Bini has an empty rule; it should carry 'no contrastive word stress; tonal (six tones); phonetic prominence follows tone glide, pitch, length, sonority and utterance position'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bini is a tone language (six phonemic tones, p. 51) with no phonemic (contrastive) word stress. Loudness is purely phonetic and predictable: it is greatest on syllables with a tone glide, then scales with pitch height (top > high > mid > low > flat > bottom), vowel length, vowel sonority (open vowels loudest), and position, earlier syllables in an utterance being louder than later ones (downdrift of pitch and loudness across a breath-group). No syllable of the word is designated as the stress-bearer.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such. Wescott gives a gradient scale of 1-6 'stress units' by tone-glide type (p. 30) and by level tone (p. 31), says a phonetic syllable is 'a sequence of allophones sharing one but not more than one maximal stress' (p. 36), and adds in Section 7 (p. 51-52) that low tone, because of its subphonemic down-glide, 'has more stress than any other tone', all other tones having 'stress consonant with their pitch'.
new_statements.exceptions: Vowel quality (oral vs nasal) has no correlation with stress (p. 33). In 'paraphonic' utterances where consonants are syllabic, a sonority ranking of consonants governs stress; stops never carry stress (p. 33). In English loanwords, a high-vowel syllabic develops next to the syllable that carried English primary stress, e.g. 'cook', 'school' (pp. 105-106). Tone inventory varies by speaker: only about one in ten speakers has all six tones, about three in ten have four (p. 52).
new_statements.identity_note: Wescott 1962 describes Bini (Edo) as spoken in Benin City; he notes sociolectal variation in the tone inventory (about one in ten speakers with six tones, about three in ten with four, mid having merged), which does not affect the stress statement.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bini has no phonemic (contrastive) word stress. Loudness is purely phonetic and predictable from tone glide, tone height, vowel length, vowel sonority and linear order (earlier syllables louder, other things equal); the phonemic prosodic system is tonal (six phonemic tones in Wescott's analysis). Parts 2 (Morphology) and 3 (Lexemics) contain no stress or accent statement at all; they treat tone ('lexical intonation', fixed vs free tone classes) only.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None; stress is not phonemic, so no primary/secondary distinction is posited. Phonetic loudness is graded (Wescott's 1-6 'stress units') by tone and vowel properties, not by position in the word.
new_statements.exceptions: None as exceptions to a stress rule. Wescott notes phonetic stress as a cue to syllable count (Section 4, p. 36: a syllable is 'a sequence of allophones sharing one but not more than one maximal stress') and that English loanwords develop a high vowel adjacent to the syllable that carried English primary stress (p. 105-106), neither of which posits Bini word stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Wescott describes Bini (Edo) of Benin City as spoken by his informants at MSU c. 1960-62; no dialect restriction relevant to stress. The HathiTrust record is the 1963 New Haven College issue of the same three-part grammar (v.1 = Phonology).

sources.note: Ch. 2 Section 3 'Stress' (pp. 30-33): Bini 'has no phonemic stress' but does have phonetic stress, which correlates (in order of importance) with tone-glide, pitch height, vowel length, vowel sonority and priority of occurrence (other things equal, the first vowel of a word is loudest); stress is a clue to syllabification. Section 7 'Prosodic Phonemes' (p. 56ff) treats tone (six phonemic tones) and quantity as the prosodic phonemes; low tone is loudest because of its subphonemic down-glide.

sources.note: First-hand tonal analysis: Edo (Bini) is a classic downstep system with two basic tones (H, L); downstepped H arises from a lost L; argues (after Amayo 1976) for a downstepped Low occurring where a L follows a deleted L, the same environment where H is downstepped; distinguishes true HL/LH contour glides from a 'non-low falling' (raised-Low-like) tone produced by H spreading onto L (HL -> H HL); Edo associative-construction data.
